procedural_history.impugned_order: Award dated September 10, 1965, of the Labour Court, Jullundur in Reference No. 157 of 1959, directing reinstatement of Respondents 2 to 24 and other remedies.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Respondents (presumably the workmen) filed a Writ Petition in the High Court of Punjab against the initial Award of the Labour Court. A Single Bench of the High Court held that the workers had not abandoned their services, but that the management had terminated them, and remanded the case to the Labour Court for a fresh decision. The management filed a Letters Patent Appeal against this decision, but it was later dismissed as withdrawn.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The management (Oriental Textile Finishing Mills, Amritsar) appealed to the Supreme Court by Special Leave against the Award dated 10-9-65 of the Labour Court, Jullundur.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal is accordingly allowed except for the Award in respect of Surat Singh, which is maintained.
directions: There will be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the termination of employment of the Respondents in the circumstances of the case without an enquiry was justified.

facts: A group of workmen (the Respondents) went on strike after some of their co-workers were suspended.
The management and Labour Officers tried to persuade the striking workers to return to duty.
The workers refused to return unless the suspended workmen were also taken back.
The management issued notices giving the workers a deadline to rejoin, failing which their names would be removed from the muster roll.
The workers did not return, and the management terminated their employment by removing their names from the roll.
Crucially, the management did not hold a domestic inquiry into the workers' alleged misconduct before terminating them.
It was conceded at the outset that for one specific employee, Shri Surat Singh (Respondent No. 16), there were no applicable standing orders, making his termination invalid.
law: The Supreme Court affirmed the principle that even if an employer does not conduct a domestic inquiry before terminating an employee, it can still justify its action by presenting evidence of the employee's misconduct directly before the Labour Court or Tribunal.
Merely going on strike does not automatically justify the termination of an employee's services.
However, a persistent and obdurate refusal by workmen to join duty, especially after the management has made reasonable efforts to persuade them, can constitute misconduct that justifies termination.
It is not necessary in every case to prove overt acts like intimidation or violence to justify termination for strike-related misconduct.
application: The Court split its decision based on the different circumstances of the employees.
For Shri Surat Singh, the Court accepted the concession that his termination was invalid because no standing orders applied to him. Therefore, his reinstatement was upheld.
For the other respondents, the Court found that the management had successfully justified the terminations before the Labour Court, even without a prior domestic inquiry.

The Court determined that the workers' refusal to return to work was 'persistent and obdurate'. The management had given them multiple notices and over a month to rejoin, but the workers remained adamant.
The Court concluded that this persistent refusal constituted misconduct. Therefore, the management's action to terminate their services was reasonable and not improper.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided the issue partly in favor of the workers and partly in favor of the management. It held that the termination of one employee, Shri Surat Singh, was not justified because it was conceded that no standing orders applied to him. However, the termination of the other respondents was justified because, despite the lack of a domestic inquiry, the management successfully proved to the Labour Court that the workers' persistent and obdurate refusal to return to work constituted misconduct.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the termination of employment of the Respondents in the circumstances of the case without an enquiry was justified.
appellant_arguments: The management took every possible step to persuade the workmen to return to their duties, but the workmen were adamant and abandoned their service.
There was a persistent and obdurate refusal by the workmen to join duty, without any sufficient cause.
The strike was illegal, and it was not necessary for the management to prove that the respondents were guilty of overt acts of intimidation, incitement, or violence.
Even if no domestic enquiry was held, the Labour Court had to adjudicate the dispute and could find the termination justified based on the misconduct (the illegal strike) proven before it.
respondent_arguments: The workmen had not abandoned their services; rather, it was the management that had terminated their employment.
The termination of services without a proper enquiry was not legally sustainable.

cases.case_name: Express Newspapers (P) Ltd. v. Michael Mark & Anr.
cases.principle: If employees absent themselves from work because of a strike in enforcement of their demands, there can be no question of abandonment of employment by them. If the strike was illegal, the employer could take disciplinary action against the employees under the Standing Order.

cases.case_name: Punjab National Bank Ltd. v. Its Workmen
cases.principle: Even if a strike is illegal, dismissal orders passed by the employer could also be illegal (e.g., for contravening Sec. 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act). The employer must still justify the dismissal on its merits before the Tribunal, as the Tribunal's jurisdiction is not limited to merely inquiring into the contravention of Sec. 33.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If management does not hold a valid domestic inquiry before terminating an employee's services, it can still justify the termination during industrial adjudication by producing satisfactory evidence of misconduct. The termination of workmen for participating in an illegal strike is justified if it is proven that the workmen persistently and obdurately refused to return to work despite management's reasonable efforts to persuade them; it is not necessary for the management to additionally prove overt acts of violence or intimidation.
obiter: Workmen can resort to a strike to press for their demands without severing the employer-employee relationship.
Management has the right to continue its work during a strike, which includes employing other workmen.
The mere illegality of a strike does not, by itself, justify the termination of the striking workmen's services.
The evidence required to justify an action against a workman before an industrial tribunal is not as stringent as that required in a court of law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: If management does not hold a domestic inquiry before terminating an employee, or if the inquiry held is invalid, it can still justify the termination when the matter is referred for industrial adjudication. The management can support its order by producing satisfactory evidence and proving the misconduct before the Labour Court or Tribunal. In this case, the management successfully proved the misconduct of the respondents—specifically, their persistent and obdurate refusal to join duty during an illegal strike—before the Labour Court, thereby justifying the termination of their services.
legal_tests_applied: When a domestic inquiry is not held or is found to be invalid, the management has the right to support its order of discharge, termination, or dismissal by producing satisfactory evidence and proving the misconduct before the industrial adjudication body (e.g., Labour Court).

The evidence required to be produced before the Labour Court to justify the action is not as stringent as that required in a Court of Law, but it must be such as would satisfy the Tribunal that the order of termination is proper.
why_appellant_lost: The provided text does not contain the court's reasoning for maintaining the Award in respect of Surat Singh, which was the only part of the appeal the appellant lost.
why_respondent_won: The provided text does not contain the court's reasoning for maintaining the Award in favour of Surat Singh. The respondents' primary legal argument—that termination without a proper enquiry was inherently not legally sustainable—was rejected by the court as a general principle.
policy_considerations: While workmen can resort to a strike to press for their demands without severing the employer-employee relationship, it is an equally accepted principle that the work of a factory cannot be paralysed and brought to a standstill by an illegal strike. In such circumstances, the management has the right to carry on the work of the factory, which may include employing other workmen and justifying its actions on the merits in a subsequent adjudication.
